text: In her 1902 American school manual, Mattie Phipps Todd places felt and paper mat weaving before loom work. The flat strips make the alternating interlacement visible, allowing children to learn the principle before managing yarn on a frame (Chapter II).

text: Todd’s 1902 school loom instructions prefer one continuous warp string over joins made with a weaver’s knot. She reports that even a properly made knot may fail under weaving tension, so the uninterrupted thread reduces an avoidable weak point (Chapter IV).

text: Todd places the first and last warp threads directly over the frame’s side rods and takes the weft around both rod and thread. In this American teaching loom of 1902, the rods act as temporary guides for straight edges (Chapter IV).

text: Todd’s 1902 weaving manual tests warp tension by touch: it should feel firm but yield slightly under the hand. Too little tension makes the work uneven; too much crowds the weft and makes the final inches difficult to weave (Chapter IV).

text: For a pattern placed beneath the warp, Todd draws a grid matched to the actual loom notches instead of relying on standard squared paper. Her 1902 classroom method makes the drawing’s spacing correspond to the threads that will realize it (Chapter IV).

text: Todd describes weaving long strips on a short school frame by freeing and moving the finished section down, then fastening the remaining warp again at the top. The loom fixes the working area without fixing the final length (American manual, 1902, Chapter IV).

text: Todd’s 1902 manual joins fine wool and cotton wefts by overlapping their ends through several identical warp crossings, preferably inside the mat rather than at an edge. The splice avoids a projecting knot and keeps both faces smoother (Chapter VII).

text: For rag or silkoline strips, Todd overlaps the ends and stitches them with matching thread. Her 1902 school craft manual distinguishes this flat sewn splice from the overlapping method suited to finer yarns (Chapter VII).

text: Todd marks the start of a rug’s second end stripe by measuring the first stripe’s distance from the opposite end. In her 1902 classroom practice, colored ties on the warp preserve the measurement while weaving continues (Chapter VIII).

text: Todd’s 1902 American manual weaves doll-scale face and dish cloths from bias-cut white cheesecloth. She deliberately leaves the weft less closely packed to keep the cloth soft, then conceals warp ends or binds the edges with tape (Chapter X).

text: Todd constructs small raffia boxes from separately woven panels. Rattan stitched around the panel edges stiffens them before the panels are joined, so a flat school weaving becomes a three-dimensional container (American manual, 1902, Chapter XI).

text: Todd’s doll-sized Tam O’Shanter starts as a woven square. Its corners fold toward the centre and are sewn or laced to form the head opening, with a tassel added on top; the 1902 school project turns a flat piece into clothing (Chapter XII).
